title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
description: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a
body: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training -  those dubbed as Neets - this week. Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time. Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview."With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications."It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances. But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this. Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says."It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting. But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

schema.headline: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond

title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft
description: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv
body: Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.Writing in the Telegraph, external, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.In October, Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK government would "seek to progress" Germany joining GCAP. He said the partnership could also support cooperation on issues including "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

schema.headline: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft

title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
description: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.His family announced th
body: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

schema.headline: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89

title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
description: She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia."I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation
body: She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia."I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret."We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.The singer, whose hits include Flowers and Party in the U.S.A, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony

title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
description: Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be
body: Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union. Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations. The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government. "It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want. "And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit. "When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head. "He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer. "Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

schema.headline: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page says she nearly messed up Gavin and Stacey audition
description: Joanna Page has said she nearly messed up her Gavin And Stacey audition after failing to do a Cardiff accent.The 49-year-old rose to fame after starri
body: Joanna Page has said she nearly messed up her Gavin And Stacey audition after failing to do a Cardiff accent.The 49-year-old rose to fame after starring as Stacey in the BBC comedy opposite creators James Corden and Ruth Jones.Page, from Swansea, told campmates on ITV's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here! that she had initially read some scenes for Jones using her actual accent.She recounted that she was then asked to do it in a Cardiff accent, as that was where her character was supposed to be from, but Jones told her it sounded "awful" and to "just be you".Speaking about her preparations for the life-changing audition, she said: "I remember reading the script, Ruth and James had written it and I remember thinking, 'This is me, she is me, I can do this'."Page said she got the offer for the part in the Bafta-winning sitcom two weeks after being rejected from a West End show.She said: "I was working in a shoe shop in East Dulwich and I'd just missed out on getting the part in Dirty Dancing The Musical."And so if I'd have got that, I never, ever would have done it."Page also recalled her first impression of Mathew Horne - who played Gavin in the series - during their chemistry read and said "he seemed really cool, and I thought I'm not cool and I'm just a nerd".The hit series aired for three seasons from 2007 until 2009 followed by Christmas specials including the series finale in 2024.

schema.headline: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page says she nearly messed up Gavin and Stacey audition

title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
description: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Ko
body: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency. "Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating. His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong."I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.All this made even honest test takers paranoid.Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

schema.headline: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal

title: Special educational needs: Limavady teenager's alpacas helping children with additional needs
description: Image caption, Hayden has opened his alpaca farm for the benefit other childrenByDean McLaughlinBBC News NIA teenager who has autism and ADHD has help
body: Image caption, Hayden has opened his alpaca farm for the benefit other childrenByDean McLaughlinBBC News NIA teenager who has autism and ADHD has helped turn his alpaca farm into a safe haven for other children with special educational needs.Hayden Geraghty, 16, and his mother Caroline welcome children and adults to their farm in Limavady, County Londonderry, for what is known as alpaca therapy.The farm at the foot of Binevenagh mountain also has Valais Blacknose sheep, and Hayden regularly takes the animals to visit his school.Health experts and charities have said working with alpacas can be therapeutic, reduce anxiety and improve someone's mental and emotional well-being."I have seen a serious change in Hayden since the alpacas came into his life," Caroline Geraghty told BBC News NI."Hayden went backwards a lot during the Covid lockdown. A friend mentioned an alpaca farm to visit in Malin Head in Donegal. Everything changed for Hayden after that visit and we had to get our own."The alpacas are very much in tune and are inquisitive. The way Hayden's mood changes around the alpacas and the sheep is incredible. I even find myself more relaxed around them."Image caption, Hayden and his mother Caroline take the alpacas to his schoolHayden and his mother take the alpacas to his school, Rossmar Special School in Limavady, where children get to pet the alpacas and walk them."We do not charge money for this. It's very much about spreading the love to other neurodivergent children and adults," Caroline added."This is a safe haven for people. Hayden also takes part in agricultural shows and exhibitions now and his new confidence is mind blowing."Image caption, The alpacas have proven to be popular with the children at Rossmore Special SchoolHayden told BBC News NI he "feels great and relaxed" when working with the animals."I spend time with the alpacas a lot and feed them. It makes me feel really happy because the animals are calm."Children with special needs come here to feed them and it's like a therapy session for them."I have taken the alpacas into my school and it was really good."Rossmar Special School vice-principal Laura Fisher said she had seen an "immediate lowering" of pupils' anxiety and stress levels when they spent time with the animals."Alpacas have been coming for about a year now and it's been great to see how happy it makes pupils," she added.Image caption, Laura Fisher said the alpacas have brought joy to the children at her schoolHer view is backed by Ema Cubitt, Northern Ireland's independent autism reviewer, whose role is to monitor care and services for autistic people and their families."Research has shown that animal-assisted activities can offer benefits for emotional wellbeing, communication and social connection," she says."We should never underestimate the value of simply bringing happiness and enjoyment into a child's school day."What makes this story stand out is that it began with something this young man loves, and he's now sharing it with other children."Sometimes the best opportunities in education begin by listening to young people and following their lead."Image caption, Hayden feels proud that his family are helping others through their animalsSpending time with animals can have real benefits for our health, says Northern Ireland's mental health champion Prof Siobhan O'Neill."Interacting with them can help reduce stress and anxiety, encourage positive emotions, and create a sense of comfort and companionship," explains O'Neill."For children and adults alike, particularly those who may experience difficulties with social interaction or emotional regulation, these experiences can be hugely valuable."The pleasure of caring for and spending time with an animal can help people feel more settled, confident, and happy."Hayden is now keen to expand his herd of alpacas and sheep to help more young people like himself."I'm very proud of myself and all I have achieved," he says."I'm also proud that we are helping others."

schema.headline: Special educational needs: Limavady teenager's alpacas helping children with additional needs

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
description: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when
body: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight."She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue."He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen"."She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did."That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent."Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina."And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025. He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.But she kept any of those fears from Jenny."I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door."I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.He remains behind bars awaiting trial.A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her."Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.""She's doing great for what she's gone through."They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen."I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

schema.headline: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

title: AI is being used to clone real people's videos
description: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is
body: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI charactersFigure caption, Watch: Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycatsByMarco Silva Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.Image source, BBC/Sophie LloydImage caption, Guitarist Sophie Lloyd (left) and "Mila Vasari""A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.Image source, BBC/Kjetil Krogstad"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money."What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult  content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."Image source, BBC/Grace RobertsDozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission."I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress."I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered.""I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people."And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says."It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

schema.headline: AI is being used to clone real people's videos

title: Tony Pulis column: How does Mauricio Pochettino prepare for his first Man Utd game?
description: Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United, where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wond
body: Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United, where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.West Brom's first game after I was appointed manager was a draw with West Ham on New Year's Day 2015.I sat in the stands at Upton Park with my son, Anthony, who was concerned how different the Albion team was compared to Crystal Palace, the last team I had managed in the Premier League.He was right to worry about it, but we still found a way - a totally different way of playing, but still a way to win that suited the group.My initial aims after arriving at any club mid-season were pretty direct and also pretty basic too.The staff I inherited did not just know the players, they were also the first group who had to understand my objectives and also my principles - like the work ethic I expected, for example.Irrespective of what they were used to doing, it was imperative they followed my lead.One of the clubs I arrived at were struggling at the foot of the table and also suffering from a glut of injuries.In my opinion, the players were taking advantage of a very honest and hard-working medical department, who were quite accommodating on the treatment times for the lads.I changed that immediately, so injured players were treated at 9am, 2pm and 4pm, with sessions in-between those times for strength and recovery workouts.This did not go down well with the players because it impeded on their social lives and, in one case, a player whose injury record was not exactly brilliant came to me complaining that his wife expected him to pick his children up from school and being asked to be in at 4pm affected his private life too.I did not budge, and funnily enough the player in question recovered quite quickly - as did the majority of the other injured players.Asking injured players to be at the training ground all day was by far the best way of getting them fit, in my experience, and the medical departments I managed were all working well past 4pm anyway so it was no hardship to them.Just on that side of things, I would sometimes get the feeling some medical departments thought that, if they weren't treating players, then they weren't doing their jobs.That was completely the opposite to how I saw it. I would congratulate people for having empty treatment rooms and applaud them for their work.Treatment rooms are comfort areas that certain players would always gravitate to, to have a kiss and a cuddle if they are feeling sorry for themselves for not being in the team. That's one of the first things that has to change, because you cannot give your players any excuses or hiding places if they are not performing.Similarly, I have always laughed at new managers who take over in mid-season and complain about the lack of fitness in their squad.I am sure I have done it myself at some point, but then I had a reputation of managing extremely fit squads of players and it was always an area I studied really closely.Early on in my management career, we weren't blessed with the advanced fitness equipment used in football today, but I was still able to quickly arrive at the level I believed the players should be at.How? Simple. Firstly, I had my own fitness runs that were tried and tested but, also, I knew that if during a fitness session they weren't moaning and sweating, they weren't working hard enough.Privately, you can realise very quickly when and which additions to the squad are needed.Pochettino will no doubt be thinking about that at United already, but he has 10 games in the Premier League and Champions League before the January transfer window opens.In the meantime, everything has to be geared towards winning games. I always knew I needed to do that quickly, because it helps the players believe in what I was doing, which is important too.I've outlined my principles I held at every club above, and they never changed, but my playing principles were determined by the quality of the group I inherited.My big strength as a coach was relaying what I needed from every individual player in the team, and I'm afraid repeated sessions were the go-to remedy to get there.I apologise to all the lads who had to put up with me barking out the same commands, day after day, until even our weaker links would remember their individual and the team's plays in and out of possession.It goes without saying that with United changing their manager again, their supporters will be hoping for an immediate bounce in respect of results and performance.Michael Carrick's results when he took the reins at Old Trafford at the start of this year were fantastic, with six wins and a draw in his first seven league games - including victories over Manchester City and Arsenal.As a consequence, he steered United from mid-table to third place and Champions League qualification.Even if Pochettino delivers something similar then, for that success to last, he has to be able to have more control over the future recruitment into the club.That has been an absolute disaster recently, and I don't believe blame for it can be thrown in Carrick's direction. In fact, Pochettino should use what has happened as his argument for what needs to change to achieve his aims of bringing United out of recession and on the road to recovery.Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

schema.headline: Tony Pulis column: How does Mauricio Pochettino prepare for his first Man Utd game?

title: Nations Championship: England will not get carried away by win against All Blacks - Matt Dawson
description: In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the
body: In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.However, they will want to back it up.A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.Figure caption, England beat New Zealand by record margin'An enormous statement about English rugby'Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.I can name at least two quality options in every position.Fresher France my favourites France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.I would have loved England to be competing for a trophy on this final weekend, but France have been the more consistent side.The tables have turned, and suddenly the top teams in the world are in the northern hemisphere.That is the magic of this new tournament. Everything can change in the space of a week.Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Alastair Telfer.Figure caption, France thrash Argentina to reach Nations Championship final

schema.headline: Nations Championship: England will not get carried away by win against All Blacks - Matt Dawson

title: Las Vegas Grand Prix result: Max Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.The leading group
body: Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.The key stories of an engrossing race were:Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstancesAnother dip in a dreadful season for RussellMore controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other"How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s."Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier, but a ninth-place finish was not what he was expecting.The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.Antonelli had lifted off the throttle because he wanted to stay behind Verstappen and attack him later, but in so doing had triggered a setting in the engine defined by the rules that left him without battery power.It deprived him of the chance to deploy what Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff said was a "secret" deployment strategy on the final lap that he felt would have kept Antonelli ahead through the final corners after passing Verstappen down the Strip.Instead, it gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

schema.headline: Las Vegas Grand Prix result: Max Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide

title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
description: The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consum
body: The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed."That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget.The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter."For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies."Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said."Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.

schema.headline: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
